transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… yeah. I came in because I can’t really stop thinking about how the left side of my face looks. It’s like… in every ID photo, or when I’m on camera for an online class, I notice it immediately—my nose looks crooked to me, and my jaw looks uneven, like it’s shifted or something.

And I know people tell me they don’t see it, or they say it’s “just the angle,” but it doesn’t feel that way to me. It feels really obvious, like before anyone notices anything else about me, they’re seeing that my face looks off. Even in the CNC lab, I feel like everyone is noticing my face before they notice my work or what I’m doing. It’s gotten to where I just can’t get it out of my head.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking mirrors, avoiding photos, or trying to cover your face—to deal with these concerns about your appearance?

Yeah… I do. A lot. It’s kind of embarrassing how much of my morning gets taken up by it.

Before I leave for school, I’ll go into the bathroom and check my face in the mirror, especially from the left side, and then I’ll open my phone camera too because somehow the mirror and the camera don’t feel like they show the same thing. So I’ll be turning my head a little, checking different angles, leaning closer, backing up, trying to see if my nose looks crooked or if my jaw looks uneven. And then if it looks bad in one angle, I’ll try to fix my hair so it kind of distracts from it, or I’ll change shirts because certain collars or colors make me feel like the asymmetry stands out more.

Sometimes I’ll ask my mom before I leave, like, “Does my face look weird today?” or “Does this side look off?” And she’ll usually say no, but I don’t really believe it for more than a minute. I’ll go back and check again anyway.

It can take so long that I’m late or I miss lab, which is stupid because I know I’m supposed to be there, but I get stuck. And even if I do make it, I’m already exhausted from all of that, so I’m sitting there in the CNC lab trying to focus, but I feel wiped out before the day even really starts.
Do these concerns about your face ever make it hard for you to go to school, interact with others, or take part in activities you used to enjoy?

Yeah… it’s been affecting basically everything, honestly. School is the biggest one. I’ve missed CNC labs and shop shifts because I just couldn’t get myself out the door. Like I’ll be standing there ready to leave, or supposed to be ready, and then I’ll catch my face from the side or open the camera one more time, and then suddenly I’m stuck trying to figure out if I can go in looking like that.

And it’s not like those labs are optional, you know? They’re tied to the program and the placement stuff. My faculty mentor actually told me my work placement could be in jeopardy if I keep missing time, which… I know that should snap me out of it, but it doesn’t always. It just makes me feel worse and more embarrassed, and then I don’t want to show up after missing things because I feel like people are going to look at me even more.

And socially, yeah, I’ve kind of backed out of things. I stopped playing soccer, which I used to really like. I also stopped volunteering. It’s not because I stopped caring about those things—it’s more that I don’t want people looking at me, especially from certain angles or in bright light or when we’re all standing around talking. I end up thinking more about my face than whatever I’m supposed to be doing, so I just avoid it.
Can you describe how these concerns about your face make you feel emotionally, and have you ever felt like they are interfering so much that you can’t live your life the way you want to?

Emotionally it makes me feel… trapped, I guess. Like I’m not just insecure for a minute and then I move on. It’s more like the whole day starts revolving around whether my face looks “wrong” or not. I feel embarrassed, tense, kind of ashamed, and then I get frustrated with myself because I know I’m missing things that actually matter.

Like with school, I’ve missed CNC labs and shop shifts because I literally couldn’t get myself out the door. I’ll be trying to leave, and then I check again, or I think about walking into the lab with everyone seeing me from the side, and I just freeze. And now my faculty mentor has said my work placement could be in jeopardy if I keep missing time, which scares me a lot because that’s what I’m supposed to be working toward. But even knowing that doesn’t always make it easier.

And yeah, it does feel like it’s stopping me from living the way I want. I stopped playing soccer, and I stopped volunteering too, because I don’t want people looking at me. I used to actually enjoy those things, but now it feels like I’m constantly thinking about angles and lighting and whether someone is noticing my face. So I end up not going, and then I feel worse because it’s like my life is getting smaller.
Has this concern about your face affected any other areas of your life, like your relationships with family, your performance in classes, or your ability to take care of yourself?

Yeah… it has. I mean, school is the main place where it’s really obvious, because I’ve missed CNC labs and shop shifts from getting stuck at home and not being able to make myself leave. It sounds so dumb when I say it out loud, because it’s not like I don’t know I’m supposed to go. I’ll be ready, or almost ready, and then I check my face again or start thinking about walking in and people seeing me, and then the whole thing just kind of collapses.

And now my faculty mentor told me my work placement could be in jeopardy if I keep missing time, which really scared me. That’s supposed to be the point of the program, you know? Like I’m trying to actually get somewhere with this, and then I’m the one messing it up because I can’t get out the door.

Outside of classes, I’ve stopped doing stuff too. I used to play soccer, and I used to volunteer, and I’ve basically backed away from both because I don’t want people looking at me. It’s not that I stopped liking those things. It’s more like being around people feels too exposed, and I’m thinking the whole time about what they can see instead of actually being there. So yeah, it’s affected a lot. My life feels a lot smaller than it used to.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms align most strongly with F45.22 (Body Dysmorphic Disorder), as they demonstrate preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance, repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, reassurance seeking), and significant functional impairment across multiple domains (academic, social, occupational). F33.2 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, Current Episode Severe Without Psychotic Features) and F43.22 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) were previously considered but are less consistent with the core presentation of appearance-related obsessions and compulsions.
